title: An ordinary day
goal: Describe your day from waking up to going to bed — fitting in reflexive verbs (*mă trezesc, te culci, se uită*), then sorting every verb you know into the four conjugation groups.
bekal: use reflexive verbs with their pronouns: *mă, te, se, ne, vă, se*
recognize the four conjugation groups (*-a, -ea, -e, -i*) and conjugate *a bea*
say how often: *mereu, de obicei, des, uneori, rar*, and *niciodată*, which always needs *nu*

dialogs.title: Dialogue — O zi obișnuită
dialogs.intro: Coffee break at the office. Budi yawns for the third time this morning, and Ioana starts to have doubts about his sleeping hours.

lines.text: Ești obosit azi, Budi? La ce oră te trezești dimineața?

lines.text: Mă trezesc la șapte. Mă spăl și mă îmbrac repede.

notes: **Mă trezesc.** *A trezi* means to wake someone else up; *a **se** trezi* — to wake yourself, i.e. to wake up. English uses "wake" versus "wake up" or "get up"; Romanian uses one small word in front of the verb.
**Mă spăl și mă îmbrac.** The pronoun is **repeated** in front of each verb; one *mă* can't be shared by two verbs. And *repede* (quickly), as an adverb, never changes form.

**Mă uit la televizor.** *A se uita **la*** = to look at, to watch; what you watch is always preceded by *la*, and by the golden rule of unit 6 the noun is bare: *la televizor*. Watch out: without the pronoun, *a uita* means **to forget**. *Mă uit la film* = I'm watching the film; *uit filmul* = I forget the film!

**Mă duc cu metroul.** *A duce* = to take, to carry, so *a se duce* is literally "to take yourself" — to go, to head off. It means almost the same as *a merge*, and in conversation it's heard even more often. *Cu metroul* shows *cu* again, the one preposition that keeps the article; transport is covered fully in unit 12.

**Nu se grăbește niciodată. Nu mănânci nimic?** Two negative words in one sentence aren't a mistake — they're required. *Niciodată* (never) and *nimic* (nothing) always come with *nu*. The order is fixed: *nu* + pronoun + verb.

grammars.title: Reflexive verbs
body: A reflexive verb is one whose subject is also its target — like English *enjoy yourself* or *hurry up*. In the dictionary it appears with *se* before the infinitive: *a se trezi, a se culca*. When conjugated, that *se* adapts to the subject — six subjects, five forms, because *se* serves both "he/she" and "they". The verb itself is conjugated as usual.

head: Subject
Pronoun
a se trezi (to wake up)
a se spăla (to wash oneself)
a se culca (to go to bed)

after: **It always goes right in front of the verb**, and *nu* stands in front of both: *Nu mă culc devreme. Nu te grăbești?* The subject pronouns (*eu, tu…*) can still be dropped as usual — *mă* and *te* don't replace them, so *eu mă culc* isn't a repetition.

**You already know two of them.** *Cum te cheamă? — Mă cheamă Budi* in unit 1 uses the same *te* and *mă*. There, they're the target of someone else's action ("people call me Budi"); with reflexive verbs the doer and the target are the same person.

**Many verbs have two lives.** Without *se* the action falls on someone or something else: *Spăl mașina* (I wash the car) versus *Mă spăl* (I wash, I have a wash); *Mama trezește copilul* (the mother wakes the child) versus *Copilul se trezește* (the child wakes up). Body parts being washed are linked with *pe*: *mă spăl pe mâini* (I wash my hands), *mă spăl pe dinți* (I brush my teeth).

Three more from the dialogue, each following its own group: *a se îmbrăca* — *mă îmbrac, te îmbraci, se îmbracă, ne îmbrăcăm, vă îmbrăcați, se îmbracă*; *a se uita* — *mă uit, te uiți, se uită, ne uităm, vă uitați, se uită*; *a se duce* — *mă duc, te duci, se duce, ne ducem, vă duceți, se duc*. Notice *speli* and *uiți*: once again the *-i* ending changes the sound in front of it.

grammars.title: The four verb groups — and a bea
body: A Romanian infinitive ends in one of four sounds: *-a, -ea, -e*, or *-i* (a handful in *-î*). That ending decides the group. You've already used all four; now let's line them up so the pattern shows.
after: **One twin rule to remember.** In the *-a* group the "he/she" form = "they" (*lucrează*). In the other three groups the **"I" form = "they"**: *eu văd / ei văd, eu merg / ei merg, eu dorm / ei dorm* — also *eu vorbesc / ei vorbesc* and *eu mă trezesc / ei se trezesc*.

**The *-ea* and *-e* groups differ only in stress.** In *noi* and *voi*, the *-ea* group stresses the ending — veh-DEHM, veh-DEHTS' — while the *-e* group keeps the stress on the stem: MEHR-jehm, MEHR-jehts'. *-e* verbs you've met: *a începe, a face (fac), a înțelege (înțeleg), a se duce*. The *-ea* group is small: *a vedea, a avea, a vrea, a putea*.

**The *-i* group also has two patterns**, just like *-a*: plain (*a dormi → dorm*) and with the *-esc* insert from unit 2 (*a vorbi → vorbesc, a citi → citesc, a găti → gătesc, a se trezi → mă trezesc, a se grăbi → mă grăbesc*). The ones with the insert are far more numerous. The stem can change sound too: *văd → vezi*, *dorm → doarme*.

***A bea* (to drink)** is short and irregular; learn it as a little song: ***beau, bei, bea, bem, beți, beau***. The "he/she" form is the same as the infinitive, and the rhythm recalls *vreau, vrei, vrea* in unit 4. *Ce bei? — Beau un ceai. Seara nu bem cafea.*

blocks.text: Three meals: *micul dejun* (breakfast — literally "the small lunch"), *prânzul* (lunch), *cina* (dinner). *Iau* comes from *a lua* (to take), an irregular verb that comes later; for now, learn *iau micul dejun* whole — just like English *have breakfast*. Also tell apart two kinds of "sleep": *a se culca* is **going** to bed, lying down; *a dormi* is the sleeping itself. *Mă culc la unsprezece și dorm opt ore.* Useful pairs: *devreme* (early) versus *târziu* (late); *repede* (fast) versus *încet* (slowly).

blocks.title: Mornings, București-style
items: A ***covrig*** is a bread twist or ring, topped with sesame (*cu susan*), poppy seeds (*cu mac*), or salt (*cu sare*). It's sold warm from the window of a small kiosk called a *covrigărie*, almost always near a metro entrance. It costs just a few lei: the city dweller's breakfast on the go.
Traditionally **lunch** is the main meal, often opening with a bowl of *ciorbă* (sour soup) before *felul doi*, the second course.
Among friends, the morning greeting *Bună dimineața!* is often clipped to ***Neața!*** And before bed, besides *Noapte bună!*, people say ***Somn ușor!*** — "light sleep", sleep well.

blocks.text: Frequency words sit most naturally **after the verb** or at the start of the sentence: *Gătesc rar* · *Uneori gătesc*. Remember the double negative: *niciodată* never appears without *nu* — *Nu mă culc niciodată devreme* or *Niciodată nu mă culc devreme*; the sentence "Mă culc niciodată" doesn't exist. For more precise counts: *în fiecare zi* (every day), *în fiecare dimineață* (every morning), *o dată pe săptămână* (once a week), *de două ori pe zi* (twice a day).

blocks.title: Asking about habits
items: ***Cât de des…?*** = how often…? *Cât de des gătești? — Rar. De obicei mănânc la birou.*
***Ce faci de obicei…?*** *Ce faci de obicei seara? — Citesc sau mă uit la un film. Ce faci duminica? — Dorm!*
***La ce oră…?*** from unit 7 now pairs with all the reflexive verbs: *La ce oră te trezești? La ce oră se culcă Andrei? La ce oră vă duceți la birou?*
With *doamna Popescu* the form follows *voi*, and the pronoun is *vă*: *La ce oră vă treziți, doamnă?*
